title: Veteran Actor Slams Hollywood as “Boring, Tedious” and Declares He’d Rather Live in the South【Page Six】
body:
Veteran actor Tom Berenger has taken to the public spotlight to lambaste the Hollywood machine, calling the industry “boring” and “tedious” and insisting that the allure of the West Coast has long been a misnomer for him. Speaking candidly about his decades‑long career, Berenger explained that the relentless “company town” atmosphere of Los Angeles—where everyone seems to share the same job title and converse in a perpetual echo chamber of industry talk—failed to spark his creative spirit. Instead, he says, the slower‑paced life of the American South, where he now spends most of his time, offers the authenticity and variety he craves.

Berenger’s remarks come at a moment when the entertainment world is wrestling with questions about its own relevance and inclusivity. The actor, best known for his Oscar‑nominated turn in *Platoon* and iconic roles in *Major League* and *Inception*, recounted early experiences in Hollywood that left him feeling disconnected from the glossy façade. “It was boring to us. It was tedious… it wasn’t about anything,” he said, recalling long days on set that felt more like clock‑in, clock‑out routines than artistic endeavors. He added that the industry’s focus on branding and networking often eclipses genuine storytelling, turning studios into “corporate towns” where the priority is profit over passion.

Industry analysts note that Berenger’s critique resonates with a growing chorus of talent who feel stifled by the homogenization of mainstream cinema. Over the past few years, high‑profile directors and actors have publicly expressed frustration with studio mandates that prioritize franchise formulas and data‑driven decisions. The rise of streaming platforms has only intensified the pressure to churn out content that guarantees subscriber numbers, sometimes at the expense of risk‑taking projects. In this climate, Berenger’s preference for the South—a region he describes as “rich with culture, history, and a slower rhythm”—highlights a broader yearning among creatives for environments that nurture rather than constrain artistic expression.

Berenger also touched on the social dynamics that reinforce Hollywood’s insular nature. He noted that the city’s networking circles often feel like “the same group of people talking shop,” making it difficult for outsiders or those with divergent viewpoints to break through. This perception aligns with recent studies indicating that a majority of major film and television deals still circulate within a relatively narrow pool of executives and agents, limiting diversity of thought and experience. By contrast, Berenger says the South’s more dispersed and community‑oriented atmosphere allows for genuine conversation and collaboration, free from the “echo chamber” that can dominate Tinseltown.

While his comments may appear nostalgic, Berenger is not entirely dismissive of Hollywood’s achievements. He acknowledged that the industry has produced timeless works and provided a platform for countless artists. However, he argued that the current climate—marked by relentless scheduling, relentless promotion, and a focus on franchise continuity—has eroded the spontaneity that once defined the craft. “I never liked the idea of living in Hollywood because it felt like a perpetual boardroom,” he said, underscoring his desire for a lifestyle where personal fulfillment outweighs professional accolades.

Looking ahead, Berenger’s outspoken stance could inspire more seasoned actors and creators to vocalize their discontent and explore alternative hubs for production. As tax incentives and digital infrastructure make secondary markets—from Atlanta to New Orleans—more viable, the industry may witness a decentralization that mirrors Berenger’s own migration. If the trend gains momentum, Hollywood’s monopoly on cultural output could loosen, fostering a more pluralistic landscape where regional voices flourish. For Berenger, the future is already clear: a return to the South’s slower cadence may not only rejuvenate his own artistry but also signal a broader shift toward a more diverse, less monolithic entertainment ecosystem.
